characterInteraction.description: The speaker directly addresses the camera, engaging the viewer in a conversation.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The speaker’s personal experience as both a pastor and political candidate informs her perspective. Her faith and belief in scripture guide her belief in social responsibility. The video aims to inspire viewers to engage in community service and work towards a more just and compassionate world.

narrativeProgression.description: The speaker introduces the concept of the different dynamics between political office and the pulpit.
She transitions to discussing the secular world and the challenges it presents in comparison to the church setting.
She highlights the limited resources of churches compared to the government.
She introduces her perspective on the lack of separation between church and state, drawing on a biblical example from the Book of Isaiah.
She emphasizes the responsibility of both the church and government to care for those in need.
She quotes the phrase "render unto Caesar" and connects it to the relationship between faith-based organizations and the government.
She expresses her belief in a unified heaven where denomination doesn't matter.
She desires peace and camaraderie on Earth, specifically in Washington DC.
She focuses on Washington DC's role as a model for the rest of the country.
She draws a parallel between interfaith work and the need for harmony and collaboration in Washington DC.
She critiques the “dog eat dog” mentality in politics.
She advocates for a spirit of harmony, kindness, and hope in Washington DC.
She connects the return of soldiers from war with the need for peace and opportunity in Washington DC.
She reiterates the importance of Washington DC as a starting point for positive change.
She emphasizes the need for both secular and spiritual power in Washington DC.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Being in the political office and being in a pulpit are two different dynamics.
You're dealing with the secular world versus the spiritual world.
And when you deal with the secular world, you're dealing with so many other issues that
you may not even deal with in the church setting.
And so while we have served as social services, social service agencies, we don't have the
budgets of the government to make things happen for people in our congregation.
We don't have the, we can't mass volume work as governments do.
And so there is really, to me, there is no separation of church and state.
If we look at scripture in the book of Isaiah, when Isaiah was prophesying about the one
that would come, and he said the government would be on his shoulder, that we become so blindsided
to those in need to the poor and to the orphans and to the widows, and that it is our responsibility
to take care of them.
And yes, it is not only the responsibility of the church to do that.
And the faith-based community is also responsible to the government.
Render unto Caesar, that which is due Caesar.
And so if we connect Caesar with Christ or Caesar with our faith-based organizations, we
might have a better world because we can take care of all of God's people regardless
of their denomination because I believe that there are no sections in heaven for
James, there are no sections in heaven for Muslims, there are no sections for Christians,
there are no sections for by.
I think we're all going to be in one place at one time celebrating together.
And hopefully we can have that kind of peace and camaraderie here on earth.
People look at Washington, DC.
We set the example.
We set the parameters for everyone else in our country.
And if we can set the example that there's harmony regardless of if you're tall, if you're
short, if you're black, if you're white, if you have long hair, weaved hair, no hair,
ball, it, it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter where you're from, but that
we're all in this together.
And I think it's just like interfaith work.
We're able to show that harmonious camaraderie in the nation's capital from a political perspective
and it's not just a doggy, dog world, get all you can, can all you get, and then run
away with what you can run away with.
That is not the spirit I think we should show in Washington, DC.
I think we should show harmony.
I think we should show loving kindness that there's hope for our world, that there is peace,
peace can exist.
We brought all of these soldiers back home.
We need to have something for them to do now.
We need to show the world.
And it all starts here in Washington, DC.
The president, this is the city of what is Dean Power.
And so if it's that kind of secular power, it has to be that kind of spiritual power
as well because they're part and parcel of each other.
You can't have one without the other.
That's like having the right and not having the left.
That's like in front and not having the back.
They all go together.
If there's enough, there's a down.
If it's good, it's evil.
And so it goes together.
So I think that the wider community might see Washington, DC as a place of concern for
its people and not just in Washington, DC, but globally as well.

youtube_description: An interview with Rev. Dr. E. Gail Anderson Holness, pastor at Christ Our Redeemer AME Church in Washington D.C. and candidate for DC City Council.  Here, Rev. Holness speaks about how the nation's capital should lead by example, both in faith and politics.
youtube_title: Faith in Action DC: Rev. Dr. E. Gail Anderson Holness, AME Pastor & DC City Council Candidate
